summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring and identifying common system properties on a device with a NETCONF server, including system identification, time-of-day, users, and DNS resolver settings.

eli5.summary: This is a standard form for the basic settings of a network device, such as its name, clock, users, and where to look up names.

questions: what is the ietf-system yang module
how to configure ntp with netconf yang
subtitle: A standard YANG module for a device's name, clock, users and DNS settings, plus restart and shutdown operations.

tldr.problem: Devices managed over NETCONF all have basic properties such as a hostname, a clock, local users and DNS servers, and each vendor configured them differently.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-system YANG module defines standard data nodes for system identification, time-of-day, NTP, DNS resolver, RADIUS and user authentication, plus operations to set the time, restart and shut down. A companion iana-crypt-hash module defines how stored passwords are hashed.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track data model that servers can implement piece by piece, since optional features advertise which parts a device supports. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 7317 is a Standards Track document from August 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says IANA created the iana-crypt-hash module, so new hash algorithms can be added to it through Expert Review.

sections.title: What the System Model Covers
sections.content:
RFC 7317 defines the ietf-system YANG module (YANG is the data modeling language of RFC 6020) for configuring and identifying common properties of a device that runs a NETCONF server (RFC 6241). Devices managed by NETCONF, and perhaps other mechanisms, share common properties that need to be configured and monitored in a standard way.

The module provides configuration and monitoring of system identification and of time-of-day, configuration of user authentication and local users, configuration of the DNS resolver, and system control operations: shutdown, restart and setting the time.

The RFC also uses a simplified tree notation to show the data model. rw means configuration (read-write), ro means state data (read-only), a question mark marks an optional node and an asterisk marks a list or leaf-list.
sections.eli5: Every network box has the same basic questions: What is your name? What time is it? Who may log in? This RFC writes one shared list of those questions so every box answers in the same way.

sections.title: Identification and Time Settings
sections.content:
Under /system, an administrator can set contact, hostname and location. Under /system-state/platform, read-only strings describe the device: os-name, os-release, os-version and machine. These are intended to be specific to the device vendor.

The clock is set either by a time zone name from the Time Zone Database (timezone-name, such as Europe/Stockholm) or by a timezone-utc-offset in minutes, for example -480 for UTC minus 8 hours. The offset form gives no automatic daylight saving adjustment.

An optional ntp container lists NTP servers. Each server has a name, an address, an optional port (default 123, available only if the ntp-udp-port feature is supported), an association-type of server, peer or pool, and the booleans iburst and prefer, both defaulting to false. Read-only current-datetime and boot-datetime report the clock.
sections.eli5: The device has a name tag, a note saying where it lives, and a clock. You can tell the clock which time zone to use and which time-keeping servers to listen to.

sections.title: DNS Resolver Configuration
sections.content:
The dns-resolver container controls how the device resolves domain names. It holds an ordered search list of domains to try, an ordered list of DNS server entries (each with an IP address and an optional port that defaults to 53), and two options: timeout and attempts.

The resolver sends a query to the first server in the list. If no answer arrives within timeout seconds, it moves to the next server, and after the last server it starts again from the first. Once it has gone through the list attempts times with no response, it gives up and returns an error to the calling application. The defaults are a timeout of 5 seconds and 2 attempts, and implementations MAY limit the number of servers.
sections.eli5: The device keeps a list of helpers to ask when it needs to look up a name. It asks the first one, waits a little, then asks the next, and eventually gives up if nobody answers.

sections.title: User Authentication, RADIUS and Password Hashes
sections.content:
Three authentication methods are defined for NETCONF: publickey for local users over SSH, password for local users over any secure transport, and password for RADIUS users over any secure transport. Two optional YANG features, local-users and radius-authentication, tell clients which of these the server supports. The parameters are aimed at NETCONF but MAY also be used by interfaces such as a command line or web interface.

The leaf-list user-authentication-order controls whether local passwords or RADIUS are used. Each local user has a name, an optional password and a list of authorized-key entries with an algorithm and binary key data. The RADIUS client lists servers with a default authentication port of 1812, a shared-secret and an authentication type that defaults to PAP (CHAP is also defined).

Passwords use the crypt-hash type from the separate iana-crypt-hash module. A value starting with $0$ is clear text, and the server hashes it before storing it. A value starting with another $id$ is stored as is. Ids 1, 5 and 6 map to MD5, SHA-256 and SHA-512, and the server advertises which it supports through features.
sections.eli5: People can log in with a secret key they own or with a password. Passwords are never stored as the words themselves but as scrambled versions, so even a peek at the list does not give the passwords away.

sections.title: System Control Operations
sections.content:
Three operations are defined. set-current-datetime sets the system clock, but it fails with error-app-tag ntp-active if NTP is enabled. system-restart restarts the entire system, not just the NETCONF server. system-shutdown powers off the entire system.

A server SHOULD send its reply to the client before restarting or shutting down. All three operations are marked nacm:default-deny-all, so by default the NETCONF access control model does not let ordinary users run them.
sections.eli5: There are three big buttons: set the clock, restart the whole box, and turn it off. They are locked by default so that only people with permission can press them.

sections.title: Relationship to the SNMPv2-MIB
sections.content: If a device implements the SNMPv2-MIB (RFC 3418), two YANG nodes MAY be mapped to existing objects: contact corresponds to sysContact and location to sysLocation. The RFC notes that an implementation that does this needs some way to handle differences in size and allowed characters, and that defining such a mechanism is outside its scope.
sections.eli5: An older way of managing devices also has a contact field and a location field. If a device speaks both ways, the two sets of fields may be kept in step.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be accessed over NETCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH, and the NETCONF access control model (RFC 6536) can limit which users reach which operations and data.

Writable nodes that can hurt network operations if left unprotected are the time zone, NTP, DNS resolver and RADIUS settings, the authentication order and the local user list. Readable nodes that may be sensitive include the platform information and the user list, which can reveal user names and password information. The three operations that change the time, restart or shut down the device also need controlled access.

The RADIUS use inherits the threats of other RADIUS applications. The crypt-hash type can store MD5 hashes, and the RFC says the usage of MD5 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: These settings control who can get into a device and how it behaves, so only trusted people should be able to read or change them. The old scrambling method called MD5 is not recommended.
